history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes, and I'm glad we could connect today. To help us get started, could you share a little about what brings you in and what has been on your mind lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I spend hours after my shift cleaning up the messes my coworkers left, because if I don’t they’ll just keep messing up and nobody will notice. I keep a notebook of every time someone—my managers, the researchers, even friends—said one thing and did another, and it drives me crazy that they think I’ll just trust them. I smile when I talk about it, then I get angry and think about how I quit the last job as soon as they tried to fire me, because I can’t stand anyone’s failure. Sometimes I wonder if any of it even matters, whether I’m still here or not.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you write down those moments where people let you down or go back on their word, what is it you feel you need to protect yourself from?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I sit down and write down every time someone—my boss, a coworker, even the people who gave me those questionnaires—said one thing and did another, just to have proof that they’re not living up to the standards I set. It feels like keeping a ledger of their lies, and the more I add, the clearer it gets that nobody actually meets what I expect. I’m not crying about it; I’m just making sure I have something concrete, because if I don’t, it’s easy for them to slip away and pretend everything’s fine.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When someone falls short of your standards or goes back on their word, what do you believe is their underlying motive toward you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I can’t shake the feeling they’re just setting me up, waiting for me to slip so they can write me off as unstable. Every time someone skirts a detail I add it to my list of broken promises, and I see how quickly they’ll let me clean up their mess before they give me a reason to walk away. Honestly, I could just leave the paperwork half‑done and watch them scramble, because that’s exactly what they want—proof I can’t handle it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: How does this feeling that people are setting you up or waiting for you to fail affect your closer relationships outside of work, like with friends or family?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like everyone’s just waiting for me to mess up, like the manager did when I caught Jamie’s mistake and everyone stared. It’s exhausting trying to stay ahead of them, because the moment I slip they’ll write it down and add it to the list of lies they’ve fed me. Sometimes I think I’d rather just walk out and let them think I’m scared, but then the anger spikes and I can’t stop wondering if I’m just proving them right.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back across your life, how long have you felt the need to stay on guard like this, and has there ever been a time or a relationship where you felt you could completely let down your defenses?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep going over everything—every promise, every shift they covered, every mistake I had to fix—like a ledger that never balances, and whenever someone seems to let their guard down I’m already waiting for the next slip. Even when Carla stayed late and didn’t complain, I caught her missing a barcode and it just reinforced what I already knew: people can’t be trusted. So I stay on edge, double‑checking, because the moment I think I might relax, something else reminds me that the list keeps growing.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Earlier you mentioned experiencing sudden spikes of anger, quitting jobs on the spot, and even wondering if it matters whether you're here or not—when those intense emotions hit you, how do you typically react or cope in the moment?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about how everyone just keeps messing things up and then pretends it’s fine, so I write it all down and watch them scramble when I point it out. I know if I just walked out they'd say I quit again, like they always do, but staying means fixing their stupid mistakes and feeling like I'm the only one who actually cares. It gets me mad because the same people—my boss, the researchers—always seem to have some hidden agenda, and I’m just waiting for the next time they let me down.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, welcome. I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started today, could you tell me a little bit about what brings you in and what has been going on in your life recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep moving the boxes around, trying to make the place look tidy, but the clutter never really goes away, and the hallway still feels empty without my sister's footsteps. My notes on bioluminescence are the only thing that feels alive right now, and I hope someday someone will read them and maybe use my ideas about glowing skin. I’m not sure what to do with all this—my hands know how to fix wires, but I don’t know how to fix the emptiness.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy sense of emptiness right now, especially with your sister no longer being there. Could you tell me more about what happened with your sister, and whether this feeling of emptiness is something recent or something you have experienced for a long time?

history.speaker: self
history.text: It feels like the whole flat is heavier now, like the shelves are still holding all those glow‑in‑the‑dark pages but the light is dimmer without her. I keep moving the boxes around instead of actually sorting them, because I don't see any point in cleaning up when the silence is so loud. I tell myself I'm just numb, but sometimes I wonder if the papers I’ve collected might be the only thing that still shines in this place.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of the bond you shared with your sister, what have your relationships with other people in your life typically looked like?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep going back to the jars and the notes, because they're the only things that still make sense to me; the apartment feels empty now, and I’m afraid if I tell anyone more about the mess the landlord will just throw me out. I know I should have called someone sooner, but every time I pick up the phone I forget who I’m supposed to talk to, and the silence feels safer than hearing a laugh that I can’t hear. The glow of the bioluminescent samples is the only light I have left, and I’m not sure anyone would understand why it matters to me.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned feeling that silence is safer and that others might not understand your ideas—could you tell me more about what makes connecting with other people feel unsafe or difficult for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about the landlord walking in and seeing all those glowing papers piled everywhere, and it makes me want to lock the door and stay in the lab where the light is the only thing I can control. At the same time, I feel a dull ache when I think about my sister and how I hid her death, like I'm trying to protect the apartment but also protecting myself from being judged. I know I could talk about my notes, but the fear of people looking at the mess and thinking I'm unstable keeps me quiet, even though a part of me wishes someone would just listen without all the questions.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned hiding your sister's death out of fear of being judged—could you share more about what led to that decision, and whether feeling the need to hide things or keep others at a distance has been a longstanding pattern throughout your life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I held back because I was scared the landlord would see the mess and kick me out before I could finish my notes, so I kept everything quiet and tried to tidy up the way I could. At the same time, I don't really want anyone looking at the clutter either; it's easier to stay in my own world of the glowing pages than to let someone feel sorry for me. Maybe I just get tired of promising something I might not be able to keep, so I stay in the silence with my sister’s memory and the bioluminescence ideas.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back before your sister passed away, how did you typically manage work, school, or friendships, and have you always felt this strong need to retreat and hide your life from other people's judgment?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Kiedy siostra odeszła, nie chciałem nawet zadzwonić do właściciela, więc przez kilka dni po prostu przestawiałem kartki i notatki o świecących rybach zamiast sprzątać, bo bałem się, że zobaczy opiski i powie, że muszę się wyprowadzić. Wieczorami siedziałem w świetle lampy, pisząc o bioluminescencji, i choć czasem marzyło mi się, żeby ktoś przeczytał je i powiedział „to coś”, szybciej niż przyjaźń, bałem się, że tylko się śmieją. Teraz wszystko wydaje się rozmytym blaskiem – te notatki są jedynym, co naprawdę mam, a jednocześnie najtrudniej je pokazać.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Throughout your life, have you felt that your ideas and ways of seeing the world are fundamentally different or unusual compared to others, or has keeping to yourself mostly been driven by a fear of being criticized and rejected?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep the notebook with my glowing‑skin ideas tucked away in the back of that chaotic pile, because I’m afraid if I hand it to anyone they’ll point out all the holes and the landlord will find a reason to kick me out. Sometimes I think, maybe if someone actually read it, they’d laugh or call me crazy, and that thought makes my chest tighten, but then I just smile and put the papers back where they’re safe, alone in the dim light of the apartment. I know the silence is louder than any crowd, and I’m left feeling numb, like after… after my sister died, just waiting for a chance that maybe, someday, someone will see the value without tearing it apart.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes, and I'm glad we have this time to talk today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what's been going on in your life recently that led you to reach out, and how things have generally been feeling for you day-to-day?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I just keep to my apartment because it feels like the only place where the noise and the rumors don’t get in the way, even if the walls seem to whisper back sometimes. My lab notebook is still full of those odd drawings the TA called “preoccupied,” and I keep thinking about the coin I flipped—whether it says something about me or about Mom’s health—like it’s a pattern I can’t shake. I tell myself I don’t need friends, but when the hallway is empty I sometimes wonder if someone’s actually watching, waiting for me to say something.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of intense experiences right now, between noticing those connections and feeling like you might be watched. Could you share a recent example of what it felt like when you noticed one of those patterns or sensed someone watching, and how you made sense of what was happening?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like someone’s watching me in the hallway, like the lights flicker just when I walk past, and I tell myself it’s just the old building settling, but the same feeling pops up when I think about that coin toss or the sketches in my notebook. It’s hard not to wonder if the classmates are talking about me again, even though I try to convince myself it’s only my imagination. I know I could change things if I focus hard enough—like stop the earthquake or my mom’s fever—but the fear that they’ll see me as the “weird guy” still sticks around.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you think about other people, do you find yourself wishing you had close connections and felt understood by them, or do you genuinely feel more at peace and content keeping entirely to yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I’m okay staying here; the apartment is quiet and nobody looks at my sketches the way they would if I tried to be around people. Sometimes I wonder if a laugh at the door would be nice, but the thought of them seeing the drawings and calling me “weird” scares me more than the silence. I keep flipping that coin for everything, even for how I feel, because it feels safer than actually having to talk about it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Has this way of noticing special patterns and feeling different from others been something you've experienced for most of your life growing up, or is it something that has developed more recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep seeing the same strange symbols in my notebook and it feels like a warning, like the coin toss wasn’t just a joke and somehow connects to Mom’s illness. People call me weird, and I can’t shake the feeling that they’re watching, waiting for me to slip up because of those drawings. I could write everything down neatly, but it just seems pointless—only I notice those patterns. That’s why I stay in my apartment by myself; it feels safer than letting anyone else see what I’m seeing.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you're dealing with all of these overwhelming patterns and stress, how do your emotions typically shift, and what do you find yourself doing to cope with those intense feelings?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I can hear everyone talking about me even when I’m alone, so I just pull the curtains and try to count my breaths until it feels quieter. I know there’s a lab report I should be working on, but the notebook is still full of those strange drawings and the pen feels like a rule I can’t follow, so I end up staring at the wall instead. Sometimes I think maybe I should go out, smile, be seen, but then the memory of the TA’s stare and the coin I flipped makes me retreat back to the corner and lock the door, hoping the noise inside will finally stop.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back over your life, what have your relationships with family, friends, or romantic partners typically been like, and have they tended to be stormy and intense, or more distant?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I often feel like everyone’s just a shadow passing by, even my mom’s voice sounds thin and far away, so I end up watching from my window like I’m not really part of anything. The rumors about me being “weird” or the whole coin‑flip thing about who I am just make me keep my distance, because I can’t trust what people say. Staying alone in my apartment feels safer, even if it means I’m left with those drawings and the thoughts that keep drifting around like ghosts.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—it's good to meet you. To help us get started today, could you share a bit about what brought you in and what has been feeling most challenging in your life or relationships lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know I’m the best carpenter they’ve ever seen, and it’s frustrating when they keep pointing out cheap wood or “mistakes” that are really just their own problems. I’ve been told I quit jobs, fought with supervisors, and even had restraining orders, but I see that as people who can’t handle how driven I am. I keep trying to prove myself, even if it means blowing up a little or walking out when they don’t give me what I need. It feels like everyone’s just waiting for me to fail, and I’m sick of it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Can you walk me through a specific recent time when someone criticized your work or a conflict escalated—what was happening, and what was going through your mind right before you blew up or walked out?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know they’re just looking for something to blame, saying the wood’s cheap and the joint’s off, but I’m the best carpenter they’ve got and I can prove it if they’d actually give me a chance. I’ve got the certificates—yeah, I showed them at the interview—and I can cut a perfect piece in a heartbeat, even if the boss keeps pushing deadlines and nitpicking everything. Honestly, I’m tired of all this nonsense; if they keep treating me like a fraud, maybe I’ll just walk out and find a place that respects what I can do.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned earlier that you’ve had fights and even restraining orders in the past—could you tell me more about what led up to those situations and who was involved?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know people love to paint me as the villain, but every time I try to fix something—whether it’s at work or at home—their jealousy and over‑reaction turn everything into a drama, like when the cops showed up after my ex‑wives couldn’t handle the fact I was better at the job than they were. The supervisors keep whining about cheap wood and “dangerous errors,” but they’re the ones who can’t keep up with a real carpenter who knows his craft. I’m just trying to hold on to the life I’ve built, and it feels like everyone’s waiting for me to mess up so they can throw a restraining order or a lawsuit my way. All I’m really scared of is losing the one thing I finally got right.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel that fear of losing what you've built, how does that usually play out between you and the people closest to you, like your ex-wives?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about losing the house and the tools, and I can’t let anyone tell me I’m a liar again—so I just push harder, act like I’m the best carpenter, and hope they’ll see I’m not the guy who quits. At the same time, I know I should actually finish the job right and keep everything tidy, but the drama and the fear of another restraining order make me want to just shut it down and walk away. I’m trying to stay in control, but the whole thing feels like it’s about proving I’m still on top, even if it means ignoring the cheap wood and the complaints.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When things have escalated to the point where the police or courts got involved, what was specifically happening that led to those actions being taken?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep hearing people say I’m the problem, like those restraining orders and the cops showing up, but honestly they’re just jealous of how good I am at this trade. Every time I walk away from a fight or a complaint, they spin it into some legal drama, and I end up looking like the villain for doing what I think is right. It feels like they’re just waiting for any excuse to get rid of me, even though I’m the only one trying to keep things safe and actually do the job right.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back at those relationships and past jobs, how do you make sense of the impact these blowups have had on the people involved and on your own life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know the guys keep harping on the loose bolts, but honestly it’s the cheap wood and the way the foreman micromanages everything that makes the mess in the first place. When I walk out I feel a weight lift off my shoulders—like I’m finally not stuck fixing someone else’s mistakes. Yeah, the guilt shows up for a minute, but it disappears as soon as I’m out the door, and I’m left thinking I’m just doing what a real carpenter would do: refuse to let bad material and bad leadership ruin the job. So I’m not the problem here; I’m the only one who sees what needs to change.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes. Thank you for meeting with me today. To help us get started, could you share what has been going on recently that led you to reach out, and what you're hoping we might address together?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been stuck in this cycle for months—lying in bed, eating junk, scrolling until I’m broke, then telling myself I could run everything myself and calling every boss an idiot. When someone tries to get close I just pull away, scared they’ll see the cracks, and the dark thoughts creep back, even though sometimes I feel this crazy surge of energy and stay up all night before crashing into a twelve‑hour sleep. And honestly, when you glance at the clock it feels like you’re judging how wasted my time is, which just makes me angry all over again.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: I appreciate you being direct with me about how that felt when I looked at the clock, and I want to make sure this remains a space where you feel respected and heard. When that fear comes up that people will "see the cracks" or judge you, what is it you worry they will ultimately see or think about who you are?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Me da miedo que vean mi apartamento y piensen que soy una carga, que paso todo el día en la cama sin hacer nada y que gasté todo el dinero en cosas que nunca usé. A veces me enojo con todo, con los jefes, con la gente que me mira, y me pregunto por qué sigo diciendo que los demás son idiotas cuando en el fondo solo quiero que alguien se dé cuenta de que estoy aquí. Pero también siento que, si me miran, ya van a decidir que soy una fracasada, y no sé si puedo evitarlo.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: ¿Este vaivén entre querer que te vean y alejarte por miedo a que te juzguen como un fracaso es algo que has vivido desde siempre en tus relaciones y trabajos, o sientes que es algo que empezó en una etapa más reciente de tu vida?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces siento que quiero demostrar que puedo, que no soy la que se queda en la cama todo el día, pero luego me asalta ese miedo de que todos vean el desastre y me digan que soy una fracasada, así que me quedo encerrada con la tele y los paquetes sin abrir. Cuando intento mandar un mensaje, el celular vibra y me quedo mirando la pantalla, pensando que ya no sirve de nada, y termino sin responder. Es como si una chispa de energía apareciera y se apague de inmediato, dejándome con esa sensación de vacío y ansiedad que nunca se va.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: En las ocasiones en que has permitido que alguien se acerque a ti, ¿cómo han solido desarrollarse esas relaciones y qué suele suceder cuando surgen diferencias o sientes que la otra persona podría alejarse?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Siento que cada vez que dejo que alguien se acerque, mi pecho se aprieta y todo se vuelve un caos, como cuando ese chico empezó a tocarme y yo me alejé, y después recuerdo al profesor que me llamaba inútil o al jefe que me hacía sentir que todo era mi culpa. Me da miedo que si no cierro la puerta, todo se desordene y termine otra vez en una pelea o en una noche sin dormir, pero también hay una parte de mí que se pregunta si estoy atrapada en ese vacío porque nunca me arriesgo. A veces pienso que tal vez debería intentar, pero luego el reloj parece mirarme y me pregunto si estoy siendo juzgada, y todo eso me hace querer volver a aislarme.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Cuando sientes esa sensación tan intensa de que las personas o tu entorno te observan y te juzgan, ¿qué intenciones o motivos sueles sentir que ellos tienen hacia ti?

history.speaker: self
history.text: No sé por qué siempre parece que todos están mirando y esperando que me equivoque, como cuando el profe me miró y pensé que era una idiota. Me da rabia que hasta usted mire el reloj y parezca aburrido, como si mi vida fuera solo un espectáculo de fracasos. A veces me siento tan cansada de quedarme en la cama y no hacer nada que me gustaría que alguien notara que estoy aquí, pero luego pienso que solo soy una carga. No sé si debería seguir intentando o simplemente desaparecer y dejar todo atrás.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Cuando aparecen esas ideas de desaparecer o ese vacío se vuelve insoportable, ¿de qué maneras sueles reaccionar o qué haces para intentar sobrellevar ese dolor?

history.speaker: self
history.text: When the room gets quiet I feel like the walls are closing in, like that night I couldn't stop staring at the ceiling and thought about just turning everything off. I know I should try to get up and do something, but every time I think about making a list I hear my mom’s voice saying I’m always a mess and I end up wanting to stay in the dark. Sometimes I picture a big party with people looking at me, but before I even get to the door I feel exhausted and the idea just fades. I don’t want anyone to see me like that—I just want the silence to stay and not have to pretend everything’s okay.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes, and I'm glad we could meet today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what has been going on in your life recently that led you to reach out for support?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know I keep laughing and saying I'm fine, but every time I lie there with this ache in my back I feel so invisible, especially when my husband just walks past without a word. The doctors call me “best‑dressed” and actually ask how I’m doing, and for a moment I feel seen, so I smile and flirt just to keep that feeling alive. It’s like I’m trying to make them listen to my story the way I used to watch boys chase me in high school, hoping someone will notice before I just… slip away.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds like feeling noticed and admired brings a real sense of comfort and connection for you. When that attention isn't there and you feel overlooked, what goes on for you emotionally, and how typical has that experience been across your relationships over the years?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep noticing how everyone lights up when I’m nicely dressed and they call me “the best‑dressed lady,” but the moment I’m lying here with this terrible back pain they barely glance my way. I laugh and make jokes about disappearing or even about the “nice and sweet” doctors, because it’s the only way I feel they’ll notice me at all. Inside, though, it’s like a cold floor under my feet—my back screaming and the surgeon’s eyes already on the next patient. So I smile, I flirt, I say I’ll just slip out, hoping someone will finally look past the jokes and actually see the hurt.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel someone is pulling away or looking past you despite your best efforts to connect, how do you typically handle those moments, and how has that shaped your closest relationships over time?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Me siento como cuando estoy en la tienda y el cliente me mira al teléfono y ni se da cuenta de que estoy allí; intento sonreír, lanzar una broma, pero dentro me pregunto si ya no le importo nada. Me da ganas de levantar la voz, de decirle “hola” como antes, pero al mismo tiempo me río de lo ridícula que sería, como cuando el doctor me sonrió y yo solo quería que me escucharan. Así que me quedo aquí, con la puerta medio abierta, esperando que alguien, cualquier persona, note que sigo aquí y no me deje caer otra vez.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that intense feeling of being forgotten or left behind takes over, have you ever found yourself doing impulsive or extreme things to keep someone close or to cope with that pain?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Me duele la espalda como si me aplastara y siento que tengo que decirle algo antes de que se aleje, aunque a veces me pregunto si solo busco que me presten atención otra vez. Cuando los doctores me llaman la mejor vestida del ER me río, pero después ese vacío vuelve a golpear. No quiero que mi marido me ignore; quiero que sienta que lo necesita, aunque a veces pienso que soy una carga. A veces me imagino que si desaparezco, tal vez ya no me recuerden, y eso me asusta.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel that heavy emptiness and worry about disappearing, have you ever had thoughts of hurting yourself or ending your life, and how do you typically get through those moments?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep telling myself it's just a joke, that I can smile and make the nurses laugh, but the pain in my back and the emptiness after my husband walks away feel like a weight I can't shake. I love when the doctors call me “best‑dressed” and actually listen for a minute, but it also makes me wonder if I’m only getting attention because I flirt or because I’m hurting. Sometimes I think about the pills, about finally making someone see how broken I am, and then I force a laugh and hope the next compliment will fill the hole for a little while.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Have you ever taken steps to act on those thoughts with pills or done other impulsive things when you felt this overwhelmed, or how has this pattern shown up in your past?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces pienso que si me tomo una pastilla y la gente me mira, como el residente que me dijo que soy la mujer mejor vestida, tal vez me sienta… viva, aunque sea por un momento. Pero luego el dolor en la espalda me aplasta y mi marido ni siquiera me mira, y me pregunto si todo eso de reír y bromear con los doctores es solo una forma de que no se note lo sola que estoy. No sé si realmente quiero que alguien se preocupe por mí o si solo estoy buscando que me llamen por mi nombre, porque cuando me ignoran, todo se vuelve demasiado pesado.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking across your life, how have your close relationships typically gone—have they tended to swing between feeling intensely close and then deeply let down or angry, or what has that pattern looked like for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces siento que todo es siempre lo mismo: el doctor me dice “descansa” y me deja sola, mi marido ni una mirada cuando me caí, y yo aquí, esperando que alguien me vea de nuevo. Pero cuando los enfermeritos me llaman por mi nombre y me dicen que soy la mejor vestida, me dan esa sensación de que al menos soy importante un momento. Me pregunto si tal vez debería cerrar la puerta antes de que vuelvan a entrar, porque siempre termino con la silla vacía. Y sin embargo, sigo buscando ese aplauso que nunca llega, aunque sé que a veces solo lo uso como una broma para que me escuchen.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—it's very good to meet you. To help us get started today, could you share a bit about what brought you in and what's been on your mind lately regarding how things are going in your life and relationships?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I was the best broker they ever had, walked out of that car‑sales floor when they started treating the job like it was beneath me, and now I’m stuck living with my mom, which is humiliating, yet I still find myself slipping into five‑star restaurants I can’t really afford. I don’t need you to read between the lines or hand me homework; I just want someone to listen without trying to fix me. Women? They’re only after free meals, and I have a lot of love to give, but the world feels full of manipulators. I know I sound bitter, but that’s the truth.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds exhausting to feel like people are constantly looking to take advantage of you rather than appreciating what you have to offer. Could you walk me through a specific time recently when you felt someone was manipulating you, and how you handled that situation?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I caught the waiter trying to slip an extra bottle on the bill and I told him flat out, “Don’t try to milk me,” and walked out, because I’m not going to let anyone pull a fast one on me again. When they asked me to cover another shift, it felt just like that time at the car lot when the boss thought I’d just roll over and take the extra paperwork, so I slammed the folder shut and left the keys on the desk. And honestly, when the resident kept nudging me to open up, I just shut down and muttered that she’d probably use me for her résumé anyway.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back over your life and relationships, has there ever been a time or a person where you felt safe enough to let your guard down and truly trust them, or has that need to protect yourself from being used always been there?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep my guard up because trusting anyone feels like handing over the keys to a car I already know will break down. My mother’s the only person I can really count on; everyone else just wants a free meal and then vanishes. I could try to let someone in—like that night at the hotel bar when the waiter smiled—but the voice in my head, Mom’s voice, keeps warning me it’ll end the same way, so I just keep up the façade and keep the fancy places as a show.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you aren't keeping up that façade or putting on a show at those fancy places, how do you see yourself, and what feelings tend to come up when you're by yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep telling myself I was the best broker they couldn’t handle, and that’s why I still splurge on a steak at a five‑star place even though I can’t hold down a job. Living with Mom, hearing her sigh when I order those meals, makes me feel like a clown pretending to be a king. I guess I’m trying to prove I’m still something, but most of the time I just hear that empty echo of the confidence I used to shout. It’s hard not to feel like a has‑been when the applause has gone quiet.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When those moments hit where you feel disrespected or that the applause has faded, how do you typically react, and have those reactions ever led to reckless behavior, explosive outbursts, or trouble with the law?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I could feel everyone’s eyes on me when the applause stopped, like they finally realized I’m just a guy living with his mother and not the top broker I used to be. It makes me want to walk out, shout something, prove I still matter, but then I hear Mom humming in the kitchen and I don’t want to ruin that quiet… so I swallow it and keep pretending everything’s fine.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of your relationship with your mother, what have your friendships and romantic relationships looked like over the course of your life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep telling myself that everyone’s just looking for a free dinner or a cheap stay, and the moment I try to be generous they disappear—except my mother, who never tallies the tabs, even if it feels like I’m stuck in a cramped room with her. I used to walk into a bar and feel untouchable after closing a big deal, but now even a smile feels like a price tag I can’t afford. Maybe I’m just tired of the whole charade, but part of me still wonders if there’s anyone out there who’d see past the hotels and the broken broker I became.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes. Welcome to our session today; to help us get started, could you share what brings you in and what's been on your mind lately in your day-to-day life and relationships?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep smiling first, even when my stomach is in knots, because it feels safer to be the “good” one than to let anyone see how scared I am of messing up—like when the professor calls on me and I just nod and hope no one notices. My dad’s voice still echoes in my head, telling me I’m never enough, so I hide the panic behind chores I promise to start but never finish, and I cling to the kids and the dog at the park because they don’t judge. I want to be independent, I really do, but I’m still waiting for the next excuse to step back before I let anyone see the mess underneath.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel that urge to step back and hide what's underneath, how has that played out in your closer relationships or friendships when people try to get to know the real you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep smiling and saying I'm fine, but inside I feel like I'm holding my breath, waiting for someone to notice the cracks. When I think about the kids at the park, they just watch and smile, and for a moment I can be myself, but as soon as the room gets too close I freeze like I did in class, afraid of saying something stupid. It’s exhausting trying to keep up the act, and I’m scared that if I let it slip, everyone will see how nervous I really am.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: How has this exhausting need to keep up an act and hide your nervousness affected your ability to form close friendships or romantic relationships over the years?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I always try to act like everything's fine, smiling and nodding, but inside I feel this tight knot in my throat that I can't shake off. Whenever I let a little tremor show, I hear that old voice from my dad saying I'm never good enough, and I just want to disappear. I love being around kids and dogs because they don’t judge, but with people I’m scared they'll see the cracks and think I'm weak. So I keep the mask on, hoping someone will notice the real me without me having to say anything.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you're completely on your own and that feeling of not being enough becomes overwhelming, how do you typically cope with those intense emotions?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking I’ll mess up again, like when I answered that question in class and everyone stared, so I just try to stay hidden and do the work quietly. At the same time I want to get out and watch the kids play because they don’t judge, but my dad’s voice is still there telling me I never finish anything, and I end up worrying about tomorrow’s lab report instead. I smile for my cousin and the kids, but inside I feel like I’m just a burden, and I’m scared that if I say anything, they’ll notice how broken I am.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When it comes to making important life decisions or managing day-to-day responsibilities, how do you typically handle choices on your own versus looking to others to take the lead or reassure you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been staring at the lab schedule and my heart just races, like when the professor called on me and everyone seemed to be looking. I want to just pick something that feels right, but then I hear that voice from my dad saying I never get it right, and I worry my cousin will think I’m useless if I mess up. Part of me says I should just go with the first option and pretend it’s fine, yet another part keeps replaying every stupid answer I ever gave. I try to remind myself that the kids at the park smile when I bring snacks, but it doesn’t stop the knot in my chest.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When someone close to you offers support or tries to help, do you tend to lean on them to take over and make decisions for you, or do you hold back and struggle on your own out of fear of being judged?

history.speaker: self
history.text: When someone offers to take over, I tell myself I’ve got it and try to smile, but then I hear my dad’s voice saying I can’t even handle it myself, and I feel my hands start to shake. I end up staying quiet, hoping they won’t notice the wobble or think I’m weak. It’s like I’m trying to hide the cracks so nobody can laugh or point them out. And deep down I’m still scared that if I let them see, they’ll just confirm what I already hear inside.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, welcome. I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started today, could you share a bit about what brings you in and what areas of your life or relationships have been feeling most challenging lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I feel like I'm just going through the motions all day—sitting at my desk, doing what my boss tells me, and even in my relationships I end up trying to be whatever someone else wants, like I did with the opera singer even though I hated it. When I think about cutting back on the pills I get this shaking and a wave of anxiety that makes me want to just take another one, even though I know it’s not helping. It’s hard to imagine doing anything different because I’m scared I’ll mess up again, so I keep apologizing to everyone and hoping they’ll see past the mess I’ve made of myself.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you find yourself shaping who you are to fit what someone else wants or constantly apologizing, what do you worry would happen if you showed them who you really are or spoke up for what you actually wanted?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking maybe I could finally just say “no” to something—like I did with the opera lessons—and not worry about what everyone thinks, but the moment I picture that I already feel the panic rise and I imagine myself reaching for another pill. I want to stop doing everything for other people, but I’m terrified they’ll see me as selfish and just walk away, so I end up telling myself I’ll just keep saying “yes” and hope it won’t all fall apart again. It’s like I’m stuck between wanting to be heard and being afraid of the silence that follows when I finally speak up.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you imagine someone walking away or finding yourself completely on your own, what is the most frightening part of that experience for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about what would happen if I had to manage everything on my own—no boss telling me what to do, no girlfriend reminding me about the little things. It scares me, because I don’t even know how to decide what coffee to order, let alone plan my life, and the silence just feels like a huge, empty space I can’t fill. I get this shaking feeling and the tears start, and I’m terrified that I’ll just stay stuck, pretending everything’s okay when it’s not.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Has this pattern of relying on others to guide your choices and take the lead been true for you throughout most of your life, or is it something that developed more recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like I’m waiting for someone else to tell me what to do, even with something as simple as choosing an email or a shirt, and the anxiety just spikes when I try to decide on my own. The pills make my hands shake, and I get scared that if I pick the wrong thing everyone will notice and think I’m useless, so I end up just following whatever script I think they expect. I know I’ve been doing that for years—pretending to like opera, doing lessons I didn’t want—just to keep the peace, but now I’m not sure how to break out of it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When an important relationship has ended or you've faced a major conflict with someone close to you, how have you typically handled that, and what did that experience look like for you emotionally?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about how empty it feels when she left, like the silence in that opera house I pretended to love, and I just sit at my desk staring at the phone, waiting for someone to tell me what to do. My chest tightens and I end up reaching for the pills again, even though I know I’m just trying to keep the panic from taking over. I want to call someone, to fill the void, but I’m scared of raising my voice or making a mistake, so I just stay quiet and hope it passes.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that emptiness and panic feel overwhelming, what kinds of thoughts or sudden impulses do you notice having, and how do your emotions typically shift during those moments?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I feel like my chest is tightening and I can’t stop thinking about taking another pill, but at the same time I’m terrified of just swallowing more and ending up stuck in the same cycle. The office feels huge and empty without my boss telling me what to do, and even deciding what to have for dinner feels impossible. I keep replaying that night at the opera—how I pretended to love the music just to keep her—while the shaking in my hands reminds me how badly I’ve been trying to hold onto something, even if it’s just a feeling of safety. I want to reach out, but I’m scared to show how lost I am.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Welcome, I'm Dr. Reyes. To help me get a sense of who you are and what you've been experiencing, could you tell me a little about what brings you in today and what life has felt like for you recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep making lists for everything—like I did with the move, counting every box and labeling each shelf—because if I don’t have it all written down I feel like something important will just slip away. I know I’ve been hard on my boyfriend, rearranging his stuff and staying up past nine just to finish my to‑do list, and I’m scared that if I let go even a single mug he’ll see how “difficult” I am. At work they call me employee of the month, but I can’t stop questioning everyone’s answers, and that same need for everything to be right follows me home. I’m trying to tell you I love him, but the anxiety about losing control keeps bubbling up, and I don’t know how to stop it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds exhausting to carry that constant pressure to keep everything so tightly managed. When you imagine letting go of that control or leaving things unfinished, what is the core worry or fear that comes up for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep worrying that if I don’t keep everything exactly where it belongs, something will slip through the cracks and he’ll notice the mess, and then I’ll feel like I’ve failed at holding the place together. At the same time, I know I’m pushing him away by insisting on those lists and rules, but I can’t shake the feeling that if I let go, the whole apartment will just fall apart. It’s like I’m stuck between wanting everything perfect and fearing that any empty space means I’ve lost control.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you find yourself questioning other people's answers at work, what goes through your mind regarding their abilities or their intentions?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep replaying the meeting where they skimmed over that clause I spent three nights cross‑checking, and it feels like they’re just cutting corners. If I don’t point it out, I’m terrified everything will crumble and I’ll be the one they call a control freak. At the same time I know I’m hanging onto every detail from the move, and maybe I’m being too rigid, but the thought of missing something important still nags at me. It’s exhausting to carry that list in my head while watching others gloss over it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When disagreements happen or things don't go according to your plan with your boyfriend, how do you typically react in that moment, both emotionally and in how you treat him?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about the lamp—he said we could toss it, but I already have a whole grid mapped out and it feels like everything unravels if I change it. I know I get frustrated when he moves things around, yet I’m exhausted from staying up late making lists and trying to keep everything perfect. I want to tell him I’ll handle it all, but then I hear his sigh in my head and I just end up standing there, counting boxes, hoping nothing falls apart.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you notice that distance or worry he sees you as "difficult," what goes through your mind regarding how you feel about yourself and the stability of your relationship?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know people call me difficult, but I can’t help feeling that if I don’t label every box and keep everything exactly where it belongs, the whole thing just falls apart. I love him, yet every time I correct where something should go, I see him pull away a little, and that scares me more than the mess would. I’m terrified of losing something important, so I hold on to the order—even if it’s hurting us both.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: How far back in your life does this need for strict order and control go—is this something that has been with you since childhood or school, or did it become more intense recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep replaying the night I labeled every shelf and counted every spoon, because if I don’t know exactly where something is, I feel like everything’s about to fall apart. At work I stay up double‑checking briefs, and at home I still make a mental list of where his mugs belong, even if it drives him crazy. I know I’m hard on people, but I can’t shake the fear that if I let anything slip, I’ll lose something important—so I just keep trying to keep everything in its place.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of this need for order and planning, have there ever been times in your life where you acted impulsively, experienced sudden swings in your mood, or did things on a whim that felt out of control?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know I’m being difficult, but when I put his old jackets on the top shelf without even checking the list, I felt a wave of panic that something would get lost if I didn’t act fast. I stayed late at the office just to finish my to‑do list, even though Alex was waiting for dinner, because I can’t stand the idea of leaving anything unfinished. And when I cut him off in therapy, it was because I was terrified the conversation would spiral into chaos and I’d lose control of how everything is supposed to be organized.
